name: Varberg
title: Varberg Hull Gauging | UTM for Timber and General Cargo Ships
description: Ship thickness measurement in Varberg for timber carriers, general cargo and small bulk ships: hold, hatch cover and coaming UTM, ballast tanks, pre-docking.
h1: Thickness Measurement at the Port of Varberg for Timber and Forest-Product Carriers
intro: Varberg, on the Halland coast of the Kattegat, is above all a timber port: sawn wood from southern Sweden's mills is loaded here for the United Kingdom, North America and other markets. The ships are general cargo and multipurpose vessels, open-hatch carriers and smaller bulkers, many of them returning for cargo again and again. Timber loading is hard on holds, hatch covers and coamings, which is where most of our requests here begin. Each Varberg job is done by technicians who travel out from India to the ship.

highlights.h: Empty holds before the timber goes in
highlights.p: Most timber ships arrive in ballast with their holds swept and empty. The hours before loading starts are the best time to gauge tank-top plating, frames and hold bulkheads, because once the first packages are stowed those surfaces stay out of reach until discharge.

Varberg's fairway is short, about one nautical mile from the approach buoy, and the port is kept free of ice through the winter. Calls therefore run close to schedule in all seasons, which makes it easier to tie the team's travel to a confirmed loading date.

Ports of Halland is building New Farehamnen, a new forestry harbour section, as the town redevelops its old waterfront. While the work goes on, the agent confirms which quay the ship will use, since access routes and working areas around the timber berths are changing.

port.h: The Port of Varberg: timber on the Kattegat coast
p: Halland's coastline is low and sandy compared with the rocky skerries of Bohuslän to the north, and Varberg sits about halfway between Gothenburg and Halmstad, with its medieval fortress guarding the old harbour entrance. Ships come in directly from the open Kattegat, so there is no long pilotage passage between islands; the trade-off is that the harbour faces the prevailing westerly winds, and a hard blow from the west can make berthing and launch work awkward. The quay runs for around one and a half kilometres, with depths suited to handysize and smaller ships drawing up to about ten metres, so the port's customers are short-sea and small deep-sea vessels rather than large bulk carriers. Since 2012 Varberg and Halmstad have been run together by Hallands Hamnar, Ports of Halland.

Timber is the core of the business. Ports of Halland handles well over a million cubic metres a year at Varberg, most of it arriving by truck and rail from sawmills in southern Sweden and leaving as sawn, packaged timber for the British market, North America and elsewhere. Other forest products and general and bulk cargo cross the same quays in smaller volumes. The ships doing this work are typically general cargo and multipurpose vessels of a few thousand tonnes deadweight, open-hatch ships with box-shaped holds that suit packaged timber, and small bulkers. Many carry part of the cargo on deck under the timber deck cargo rules, so deck plating, lashing points and stanchion sockets get as much attention as the holds.

Because timber ships come back on regular liftings, the same hulls are seen in Varberg many times a year, and their wear pattern is well known. Forklifts and crane hooks scuff tank tops and lower frames, packages stowed against hold sides abrade the coating, and hatch covers opened and closed on every call wear at their cleats, seals and coaming tops. Condensation is another factor: timber that has stood in the rain before loading gives off moisture inside a closed hold, and the steel suffers for it over time. Demand for gauging follows from this. Owners want hold and hatch condition tracked between dockings, charterers occasionally ask for proof that hatch covers and coamings are sound, and ships approaching a renewal survey need a realistic steel estimate before a yard is chosen.

facilities.h: Gauging at the Varberg timber quays and where ships dock
p: Varberg has no drydock, so all gauging here is done alongside at the cargo quays. The practical window is set by the loading plan: holds can be measured before stowage begins or in any hold the stevedores have not yet started, and hatch covers and coamings are best reached while the covers are open and the ship is not yet loading that hatch. Ballast tanks are emptied during loading, but they need ventilation and gas measurement before anyone goes in, so tank work is only realistic if the ship starts de-ballasting early or stays alongside after completing cargo.

For docking, ships calling at Varberg go wherever their owners have a yard arrangement, often in Denmark, Poland, the Baltic states, the Netherlands or Germany. A Varberg call shortly before a docking is a good time to firm up the steel list, because the holds are empty on arrival and the yard can be sent a list based on fresh readings. Gothenburg is a short drive north if a ship shifts there for repairs.
list: Timber berths along the main quay — tank-top, hold-frame and hold-bulkhead gauging before loading starts, on general cargo and open-hatch ships.
Hatch covers and coamings at the berth — top-plate, coaming and cleat-area readings taken while covers are open between loading sequences.
Deck cargo areas — main-deck plating, lashing points and stanchion sockets measured before timber is stowed on deck.
New Farehamnen forestry section — the same work as the harbour's new berths come into use, with access confirmed by the agent.
Ships lying idle at the quay between liftings — owner's condition or pre-purchase gauging with time to open ballast tanks safely.
The ship's next docking yard — Varberg readings carried forward on the TM plan, with the team travelling on to complete renewal-survey gauging.

context.h: Port state control and the rules that bear on timber ships
p: Port state control in Varberg is the responsibility of the Swedish Transport Agency, working under the Paris MoU, and the small general cargo ships that dominate the timber trade are a regular target because many of them are older and change owners and flags frequently. Hatch covers, their securing devices and the coamings beneath them are a familiar source of structural deficiencies on such ships, so documented thickness readings help an owner show the surveyor and the inspector that the steel is sound. Ships carrying timber on deck must also meet the IMO Code of Safe Practice for Ships Carrying Timber Deck Cargoes, which puts weight on deck strength, lashing arrangements and the fittings that hold them.

European rules reach these ships unevenly. Ships of 500 gross tonnage and above calling at EU ports carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, which affects many timber ships, but the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime apply only from 5,000 gross tonnage, so a good part of the small timber fleet sits outside them. That leaves the commercial pressure from charterers and the class survey cycle as the main drivers of gauging. Varberg itself is ice-free, but ships trading timber from the Gulf of Bothnia in winter need their ice belt in good order, and owners often ask for it to be gauged alongside the holds.

jobs.h: Typical thickness measurement jobs in Varberg
jobs.p: Most jobs at Varberg revolve around the holds and hatches of ships loading timber. The scope is usually agreed with the superintendent a few days before arrival, so the crew can have the holds swept, the covers ready to open and any tanks to be entered emptied in good time. Owners of ships on repeated liftings often prefer several small scopes over consecutive calls instead of one large one, because that keeps the ship trading while the data builds up. Where a ship is going to dock soon after loading, the readings are passed straight to the yard and its planners. Examples:
list: Tank-top and lower hold-frame gauging on a multipurpose ship before loading sawn timber for the UK, where forklift damage had been reported.
Hatch cover top plates, coaming tops and cleat areas measured on an open-hatch carrier after a charterer queried weathertightness.
Main-deck plating, lashing points and stanchion sockets on a general cargo ship that carries timber deck cargo on every voyage.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a small bulker approaching her renewal survey, using holds that were empty on arrival in ballast.
Ice-belt plating and frame readings on a timber ship before a winter season trading to Gulf of Bothnia ports.

logistics: Göteborg Landvetter Airport is the nearest international airport, and Varberg is reached from there by road or by rail on the West Coast Line, which also runs south towards Copenhagen Airport for teams arriving that way. The harbour is an ISPS-controlled facility, so the ship's agent arranges gate access for the named technicians and confirms the berth. The team travels from India on Schengen visas; because timber liftings are usually booked some way ahead, there is normally enough time to complete visa formalities before the ship's arrival date.

faqs.q: Can cargo holds be gauged before the timber is loaded at Varberg?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best opportunity on most calls. Timber ships usually arrive in ballast with clean, empty holds, so tank tops, frames and hold bulkheads can be gauged before stowage starts. We agree with the chief officer and the stevedores which hold is measured first, so the team stays ahead of loading and no package is delayed waiting for readings.

faqs.q: What do you measure on hatch covers and coamings?
faqs.a: Top plating of the cover panels, the coaming plates and the coaming top bars, the areas around cleats and compression bars, and the stays and brackets supporting the coaming. Wastage and grooving at these points affect weathertightness and strength, and the readings show the owner whether repairs can wait for the docking or should be done before the next timber cargo goes in.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Varberg?
faqs.a: No. Ships calling at Varberg dock at yards elsewhere, commonly in Denmark, Poland, the Baltic states or the Netherlands, depending on the owner. A Varberg call just before a docking is still useful, because empty holds and open hatches give a quick way to firm up the steel estimate, and our team can also travel to the yard to complete renewal-survey gauging.

faqs.q: Does winter weather stop gauging in Varberg?
faqs.a: Ice does not, because the port is kept ice-free. Westerly gales can delay berthing or make working on open hatch covers unsafe, and short winter days limit deck work, but measurements inside holds and tanks carry on regardless. We plan winter jobs with some margin in the team's dates and keep in touch with the agent about the ship's arrival.

faqs.q: Can a ship on repeated timber liftings be gauged in stages?
faqs.a: Yes. For ships that load at Varberg every few weeks, the TM programme can be divided into parts, such as one or two holds and their hatch covers per call, and recorded against the same plan so the results join up into a complete set. That keeps the ship in service while the owner builds the record needed for the next survey.
